name: Liège
notes: Ring of twelve Brialmont forts around the Meuse crossings; the gateway of the German right wing.

name: Namur
notes: Nine-fort ring at the Sambre–Meuse confluence; fell 21–25 August 1914.

name: Antwerp
notes: National redoubt; the Belgian field army withdrew into it on 20 August and held until 10 October 1914.

name: Charleroi
notes: Bülow forced the Sambre here, 21–23 August 1914.

name: Luxembourg
notes: Occupied 2 August 1914; Moltke's headquarters from 30 August.

name: Aachen
notes: Assembly area of the German 1st and 2nd Armies.

name: Cologne
notes: Railhead of the right wing's deployment.

name: Paris
notes: Fortified camp of Paris; the pivot the plan turned around — or, in the concept, outside.

name: Soissons
notes: On the Aisne; the German right wing dug in north of it from 13 September 1914.

name: Meaux
notes: On the Marne east of Paris; Maunoury's attack toward the Ourcq opened here on 5 September 1914.

name: Sedan
notes: Napoleon III's surrender in 1870; crossed by the German 4th Army in August 1914 — the 1870 thread's anchor.

name: Verdun
notes: Northern anchor of the French fortress line; the hinge of the 1914 front.

name: Metz
notes: German since 1871; the hinge of the German left wing.

name: Nancy
notes: The Grand Couronné heights held by Castelnau, 24 August – 12 September.

name: Strasbourg
notes: German since 1871.

name: Louvain
notes: University town on the Dyle, on the Liège–Brussels railway; burned by German troops on 25–28 August 1914, the library with it.

name: Malines
notes: Between Antwerp and Brussels; the Belgian sortie of 25 August went out from here and the town was shelled when it came back.

name: Aarschot
notes: On the Demer north-east of Louvain; taken on 19 August, the scene of the first large reprisal, retaken in the Belgian sortie of 9 September.

name: Tamines
notes: On the Sambre between Charleroi and Namur; where the German 2nd Army forced the river on 21–22 August and shot the townspeople on the 22nd.

name: Ostend
notes: Channel port; where the Belgian 4th Division came ashore from Le Havre on 27 August on its way back to Antwerp.

name: Chemin des Dames
notes: The ridge between the Aisne and the Ailette where the German right wing turned and dug in on 13–14 September 1914; the line held there until 1917.

name: Roye
notes: Picardy town on the front of the French Second Army's northward attempt of 22–26 September 1914.

name: Albert
notes: Santerre town taken as the outflanking moved north in late September 1914.

name: Arras
notes: Artois city held by de Maud'huy's Tenth Army from the beginning of October 1914; the front stopped a few kilometres east of it and stayed there.

name: Lille
notes: The largest French city near the northern front; abandoned by the French and occupied by the German Sixth Army on 12 October 1914, and held until October 1918.

name: Ypres
notes: Flemish cloth town at the centre of the last unoccupied corner of Belgium; the salient held around it from October 1914 became the most fought-over ground of the war.

name: Gheluvelt
notes: Village on the Menin road east of Ypres, lost and retaken on 31 October 1914 — the crisis of the First Battle of Ypres.

name: Langemarck
notes: Village north-east of Ypres attacked by the new German reserve corps in late October 1914, and the name later attached to the 'Kindermord' legend.

name: Dixmude
notes: Town on the Yser held by Ronarc'h's fusiliers marins and Belgian troops through the battle of the Yser, October–November 1914.

name: Nieuwpoort

names.name: Nieuport
names.period: the French and British name in 1914

notes: Where the Yser meets the sea, and where the locks of the Ganzepoot let the tide into the polders on the nights of 21–30 October 1914.

name: Zeebrugge
notes: Channel port on the Flanders coast, in German hands from mid-October 1914 — one of the objectives that made the coast worth fighting for.

name: Pfetterhouse
notes: Alsatian village at the Swiss frontier; the southern end of the continuous Western Front from late 1914 until 1918.

name: Sarajevo
notes: Provincial capital of Bosnia, annexed by Austria-Hungary in 1908. The Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife were shot here on 28 June 1914.

name: Belgrade
notes: Serbian capital, on the Danube-Sava confluence within sight of Austro-Hungarian territory; shelled by Austro-Hungarian monitors from 29 July 1914.

name: Rossignol
notes: Village on the Semois north of Tintigny where the French 3rd Colonial Division was destroyed on 22 August 1914.

name: Bertrix
notes: Where the French 4th Army's XVII Corps was broken in the woods on 22 August 1914.

name: Neufchâteau
notes: The Belgian Ardennes town the French 4th Army was ordered on; not the Neufchâteau in the Vosges.

name: Ethe
notes: Village east of Virton, fought over by the French 3rd Army on 22 August 1914 and the scene of German reprisals against civilians.

name: Longwy
notes: Small French fortress on the 3rd Army's right; besieged from 3 August and surrendered on 26 August 1914.

name: Amance
notes: Village and hill on the Grand Couronné north-east of Nancy; the observation point of the whole position and the target of the heaviest German bombardment on 6 September 1914.

name: Champenoux
notes: Village and forest east of Nancy, fought over throughout the German attacks of 4–10 September 1914.

name: Sainte-Geneviève
notes: Village on the Moselle heights at the northern end of the Grand Couronné position.

name: Réméréville
notes: Village east of Nancy from which German heavy guns shelled the city on 9 September 1914.

name: Tannenberg
notes: The village the battle of 26-30 August 1914 was named for, at Hindenburg's request, to answer the defeat of the Teutonic Knights on the same ground in 1410.

name: Allenstein
notes: Objective of the Russian Second Army's centre as it advanced north-west into East Prussia.

name: Gumbinnen
notes: Where Rennenkampf's First Army checked the German Eighth Army on 20 August 1914 - the shock that produced Prittwitz's collapse and, at one remove, the two corps sent east from the right wing.

name: Königsberg
notes: The province's fortress and capital; holding it, or abandoning it behind the Vistula, was the question Prittwitz put to Moltke on 20 August.

name: Marienburg
notes: Eighth Army headquarters; Hindenburg and Ludendorff arrived here on the afternoon of 23 August 1914.

name: The Masurian Lakes
notes: The lake belt that split the two Russian armies' advance, and gave its name to the battle of 7-14 September 1914 - the battle the two corps from the West actually fought in.

name: Petrograd
notes: Capital of the Russian Empire. Renamed from the German-sounding Sankt-Peterburg to the Slavic Petrograd in August 1914, and Leningrad in 1924. Both revolutions of 1917 happened within about six kilometres of this point.

name: The Winter Palace
notes: The imperial residence on the Neva embankment; from March 1917 the seat of the Provisional Government, and the building the Military Revolutionary Committee took in the small hours of 26 October (O.S.).

name: The Tauride Palace
notes: Seat of the State Duma, and from 27 February (O.S.) 1917 the building that held both halves of dual power: the Duma Committee in one wing and the Petrograd Soviet in another.

name: The Smolny Institute
notes: A girls' boarding school on the eastern edge of the city; from August 1917 the seat of the Petrograd Soviet, and in October of its Military Revolutionary Committee.

name: The Peter and Paul Fortress
notes: The fortress on Zayachy Island, across the Neva from the Winter Palace: arsenal, garrison and political prison, and on 25 October (O.S.) the place the signal for the assault was to come from.

name: The Finland Station
notes: Terminus of the Finnish railway on the Vyborg side, where Lenin arrived from Zurich late on the night of 3 April (O.S.) 1917.

name: Znamenskaya Square
notes: The square where the Nevsky Prospekt meets the Nikolaevsky station, and where the crowds and the troops met on 25-26 February (O.S.). Renamed Uprising Square afterwards.

name: The Putilov Works
notes: The largest metalworking and armaments plant in Petrograd, in the Narva district in the south-west of the city.

name: The Mariinsky Palace
notes: Seat of the State Council before 1917, and in October 1917 of the Provisional Council of the Republic - the Pre-Parliament.

name: Kronstadt
notes: The naval fortress and base on Kotlin Island, some thirty kilometres west of Petrograd in the Gulf of Finland; the most radical garrison in Russia in 1917.

name: Tsarskoe Selo
notes: The imperial residence twenty-five kilometres south of Petrograd, where the Empress and the children were when the capital rose, and where the family was held under guard after the abdication.

name: Moscow
notes: The old capital and the second city; capital again from March 1918. Its own October fighting ran a week longer than Petrograd's and cost far more.

name: Pskov
notes: Headquarters of the Northern Front, about 250 kilometres south-west of Petrograd. The imperial train was diverted here on 1 March (O.S.) 1917 and Nicholas II abdicated in it the following night.

name: Mogilev
notes: Seat of Stavka, the Russian Supreme Headquarters, from August 1915; where Nicholas II was, as his own Supreme Commander, when Petrograd rose.

name: Zurich
notes: Where Lenin spent the last of his exile, and where he boarded the train home on 9 April 1917 (N.S.).

name: Luga
notes: A junction on the Pskov-Petrograd railway, some 135 kilometres south of the capital, and the point the leading trains of Kornilov's cavalry did not get past.

name: Vyritsa
notes: A station on the line into Petrograd from the south, about sixty kilometres out, where the trains of the Native Division came to a stand.

name: Velikiye Luki
notes: A railway town behind the Northern Front, in the area where the 3rd Cavalry Corps lay in August 1917 before it was ordered towards Petrograd.

name: Pearl Harbor

names.name: Puʻuloa
names.period: the Hawaiian name for the lochs

notes: The fleet base on the south coast of Oahu: three lochs behind a single dredged entrance channel, which is why eight battleships could be found in one place and why a ship sunk in the channel could have closed the base.

name: Ford Island
notes: The island in the middle of Pearl Harbor, with a naval air station on it and the battleship moorings along its south-east shore.

name: Battleship Row
notes: The quays along the south-east side of Ford Island where the battle line lay moored on the morning of 7 December 1941. The position given is the F-6/F-7 moorings, where Arizona lay; it is anchored on the memorial that spans the wreck, because the row itself has no gazetteer entry.

sources.note: coordinates, via the memorial over the wreck at berth F-7

name: Hickam Field
notes: The Army's bomber base on Oahu, adjoining the naval base, and one of the first places hit on 7 December.

sources.note: coordinates, from the aerodrome node; no encyclopaedia coordinate box exists for this field

name: Wheeler Field
notes: The Army's principal fighter base, in the middle of Oahu on the Leilehua plain.

name: Kaneohe Bay Naval Air Station
notes: The Navy's flying-boat base on the windward side of Oahu, attacked on the morning of 7 December 1941.

name: Opana Point
notes: The Army's northernmost mobile radar set on Oahu, on the ridge above Kahuku, and the one that saw the first wave coming in.

name: Honolulu
notes: The territorial capital, ten kilometres east of the fleet base. The coordinate is the city centroid at the one-decimal precision the source gives, which is enough to place a label and not enough to anchor anything.

name: Hitokappu Bay

names.name: Kasatka Bay
names.period: the Russian name for the bay on Iturup, after 1945

country: Etorofu, Kuril Islands, Empire of Japan
notes: A wide, empty anchorage in the southern Kurils, a long way from anywhere with people in it — which is why the striking force was assembled there and why nobody saw it go. The English and Japanese encyclopaedia coordinates differ by about a kilometre and a half; this is the English one.

name: Kota Bharu
notes: The north-eastern corner of British Malaya, with an airfield behind the beach. The first Japanese landing of the Pacific war was made here.

name: Hong Kong
country: British Crown Colony of Hong Kong
notes: The coordinate is Victoria, the colony's capital on the island; the airfield bombed on the morning of 8 December was at Kai Tak in Kowloon, on the mainland across the harbour.

name: Agana
notes: The capital of Guam, an American island lying inside the ring of the Japanese South Seas mandate.

name: Clark Field
notes: The bomber base on the Luzon plain north of Manila, and the place where the Far East Air Force's B-17s were caught on the ground nine hours after the news of Pearl Harbor reached them.

sources.note: coordinates, from the present air base on the site

name: Iba Field
notes: The fighter base on the Zambales coast, attacked at the same time as Clark, and the site of one of the two radar sets in the Philippines.

sources.note: coordinates, from the present airport on the site

name: Midway
notes: An atoll two thousand kilometres north-west of Oahu, on the striking force's own flank on the way in — the operation order set aside a destroyer division to bombard it on the way out — and the place where the six months Yamamoto had asked for ran out.

name: Kuantan
notes: A port halfway down the east coast of Malaya. Force Z went north to look for a reported landing here on 10 December 1941 and was found by land-based aircraft on the way back; the sinking was some way out to sea, and this pack places the event at the town rather than write a position it could not source.

name: Brest-Litovsk
notes: The fortress town on the Bug where the peace of 3 March 1918 was negotiated and signed. The Red Army took it on 1 August 1920 on the way to Warsaw and lost it again on 21 August.

sources.note: the dates in this note; the chronological table and narrative

name: Omsk
notes: The Trans-Siberian junction that was Kolchak's capital from November 1918 until the Red Army took it on 14 November 1919. Chamberlin calls it the largest town in Western Siberia; the Czechoslovaks occupied it on 7 June 1918.

name: Irkutsk
notes: Where the retreat down the Trans-Siberian ended for Kolchak: handed over by the Czechoslovak Legion on 15 January 1920, shot on 7 February by order of the local revolutionary committee, and put through a hole in the ice of the Angara.

name: Vladivostok
notes: The Pacific terminus of the Trans-Siberian, nine thousand kilometres from Petrograd, where the largest single group of the Czechoslovak Legion - about fourteen thousand men - sat in May 1918, and where the Japanese made a landing on 6 April 1918.

sources.note: the dates in this note; the chronological table and narrative

name: Chelyabinsk
notes: The Ural railway junction where a brawl between Czech soldiers and Hungarian prisoners of war on 14 May 1918 turned into a civil war along five thousand miles of railway.

name: Kazan
notes: Taken by the Czechoslovaks and the Volga anti-Bolsheviks on 6 August 1918 - with the Imperial gold reserve in it - and retaken by the Red Army on 10 September. Chamberlin calls the fight for it one of the most decisive of the war, and possibly the most decisive.

name: Sviyazhsk
notes: A small town on an island at the confluence of the Volga and the Sviyaga, twenty-five kilometres from Kazan, where the beaten Red forces fell back in August 1918 and where Trotsky's train stood for a month. Chamberlin calls it the Valmy of the Russian Revolution.

name: Samara
notes: Occupied by the Czechoslovaks on 8 June 1918, which made possible the Komuch - the government of members of the dissolved Constituent Assembly, and the high point of the democratic counter-revolution.

name: Ufa
notes: Where the anti-Bolshevik governments of Siberia and the eastern Volga met in September 1918 and agreed on the Directory that Kolchak's coup would displace two months later. Taken by Kolchak on 13 March 1919, retaken by the Reds on 9 June.

name: Perm
notes: The northern shoulder of Kolchak's front through the winter of 1918-19; the Red Army took it on 1 July 1919.

sources.note: the dates in this note; the chronological table and narrative

name: Archangel
notes: The White Sea port occupied by Allied forces on 2 August 1918, around which a North Russian government was organised. The Allies left in the autumn of 1919 and the government fell on 19 February 1920.

name: Murmansk
notes: The ice-free Arctic port where a small mixed force under British command sat from early 1918 guarding Allied military stores - with, while it stayed defensive, no objection from the Soviet government. At the end of June it turned aggressive and concluded a separate agreement with the Murmansk Soviet, which was not loyal to Moscow.

sources.note: the British force at Murmansk and the agreement with the Murmansk Soviet

name: Baku
notes: The oil city on the Caspian: a Bolshevik commune until July 1918, a small British force under Dunsterville from 14 August, Ottoman troops and a massacre of Armenians from 14 September, and the place where twenty-six commissars left from to be shot in the desert. The Red Army took it on 27 April 1920.

name: Tsaritsyn
notes: The Volga city that Stalin was sent to in 1918 to move grain and stayed to command. It was renamed Stalingrad for what happened there in the civil war, and is known now for what happened there in the next one.

sources.note: the dates in this note; the chronological table and narrative

name: Rostov-on-Don
notes: The seat of Denikin's government and the gateway between the Don country and the Caucasus, taken by the Red Army on 8 January 1920.

name: Novorossiysk
notes: The Black Sea port where Denikin's army came apart in March 1920: what could be lifted went to the Crimea, and what could not was left on the quays.

name: Ekaterinodar
notes: The Kuban Cossack capital, where Kornilov was killed by a shell on 13 April 1918 during the Volunteer Army's first attempt on it, and which Denikin took on 15 August 1918.

name: Kharkov
notes: The largest city of eastern Ukraine and one of the most fought-over places in the war: Red in January 1919, White on 25 June, Red again on 12 December.

name: Kiev
notes: The city that changed hands more often than any other in Europe in these years - the Rada, the Germans, the Hetman, Petliura, the Bolsheviks, Denikin, the Poles, the Bolsheviks again.

name: Orel
notes: The high-water mark of the White movement. Denikin's Volunteer Army took it on 13 October 1919, two hundred and fifty miles from Moscow, and lost it on 20 October.

name: Tula
notes: The arsenal town between Orel and Moscow - the last large place on the road, and the one that made the rifles.

name: Voronezh
notes: Fought over repeatedly in 1919: Mamontov's raiders battled its garrison for several days in September, and the Whites took it on 6 October.

sources.note: the dates in this note; the chronological table and narrative

name: Tambov
notes: The provincial capital that Mamontov's cavalry held for three days in August 1919, and the centre of the province that rose against grain requisitioning in August 1920 - the largest peasant insurrection against Soviet power.

name: Kozlov
notes: A railway town in Tambov province taken by Mamontov's raiders in August 1919; the headquarters of the Red Southern Front was there.

name: Yelets
notes: The western limit of Mamontov's raid, some two hundred kilometres behind the Red front line.

name: Novokhopersk
notes: Where Mamontov's cavalry corps went through the Red Southern Front on 10 August 1919 - a front that, in Chamberlin's phrase, was rather easy to break through.

name: Gulyai-Polye
notes: Makhno's home village and the capital of the territory his insurgent army held in eastern Ukraine, where the peasant congresses met.

name: Ekaterinoslav
notes: The Dnieper industrial city that Makhno took from Denikin's rear on 9 November 1919, at the moment the White front was at Orel.

name: Perekop
notes: The seven-kilometre isthmus that is the only land approach to the Crimea, stormed by the Red Army on 11 November 1920.

name: Sevastopol
notes: The Black Sea naval base from which Wrangel's fleet took the last White army out of Russia on 14 November 1920.

name: Narva
notes: The Estonian border town Yudenich's North-Western Army came out of in October 1919 and was driven back behind in November, to be disarmed and interned by the state that had sheltered it.

name: The Pulkovo Heights
notes: The low ridge with the observatory on it, sixteen kilometres from the centre of Petrograd, which is as far as Yudenich's advance got; he was pushed back from the suburbs on 22 October 1919.

sources.note: the dates in this note; the chronological table and narrative

name: Warsaw
notes: The Red Army's Western Front reached its outskirts in the middle of August 1920, and the counter-offensive launched by Polish forces south of the city broke it. Chamberlin's chronology dates that counter-offensive to 15 August; most later accounts date the blow from the Wieprz to the 16th.

sources.note: the dates in this note; the chronological table and narrative

name: Minsk
notes: Occupied by the Red Army in December 1918 as the German army went home, and retaken on 11 July 1920 as the offensive towards Warsaw opened.

sources.note: the dates in this note; the chronological table and narrative

name: Vilna
notes: Occupied by Soviet troops on 14 July 1920 during the advance on Warsaw. Its ownership was contested between Poland and Lithuania for the next two decades - one of several places where the Polish-Soviet war and the making of the new states were the same event.

sources.note: the dates in this note; the chronological table and narrative

name: Riga
notes: Taken by the Red Army on 3 January 1919 during the advance west into the former German occupation zone. Also the place where the Soviet-Polish peace was negotiated from September 1920 and signed on 18 March 1921, and where the American Relief Administration's famine agreement was signed on 20 August 1921.

sources.note: the dates in this note; the chronological table and narrative

name: Novo-Nikolaevsk
notes: A Trans-Siberian town in central Siberia, one of the first the Czechoslovak Legion took on 26 May 1918.

name: Penza
notes: The westernmost of the six groups the Czechoslovak Legion was strung out in when the fighting began - five thousand miles from the easternmost.

name: Krasnovodsk
notes: The Caspian port the twenty-six Baku commissars were taken to in September 1918, and from which they were carried into the desert and shot.

name: Smolensk
notes: A city on the road between Moscow and the western borderlands, behind the Red Western Front in 1920.

sources.note: the dates in this note; the chronological table and narrative

name: Ekaterinburg
notes: Where the former Tsar, his family and their servants were shot by the local Ural Soviet on 16 July 1918, days before the town fell to the Czechoslovaks and the Whites.

sources.note: the dates in this note; the chronological table and narrative

name: Constantinople
notes: Where the people taken off the Crimea in November 1920 were landed, and where the White emigration began.

sources.note: the dates in this note; the chronological table and narrative
